items.title: Nutritional Standards of Living in England and the Yangtze Delta (Jiangnan), circa 1644–circa 1840: Clarifying Data for Reciprocal Comparisons
items.note: Recalibrates the evidence into kilocalories and rejects the inference-derived statistics cited for Jiangnan's parity with England.

items.title: Establishing statistical foundations of a chronology for the great divergence: a survey and critique of the primary sources for the construction of relative wage levels for Ming–Qing China
items.note: Surveys the Chinese sources behind real-wage comparisons and places most of the evidence between guesswork and plausible conjecture.

items.title: Chinese National Income, ca. 1661–1933
items.who: Y. Xu, Z. Shi, B. van Leeuwen et al.
items.note: Estimates Chinese GDP per head from 1661 and finds a persistent decline from the seventeenth to the nineteenth century.

items.title: China, Europe, and the Great Divergence: A Study in Historical National Accounting, 980–1850
items.who: S. Broadberry, H. Guan and D. D. Li
items.note: First historical national accounts for China, dating the divergence earlier than the California School but later than older Eurocentric accounts.

items.title: Early Portuguese Data for Wage Developments in India: Kannur (Cananor), 1516-1517
items.who: P. T. de Matos and J. Lucassen
items.note: Adds wage and price data from unpublished Portuguese records, suggesting Indian real wages rose to a peak around 1600.

items.title: Poverty or prosperity in northern India? New evidence on real wages, 1590s–1870s
items.who: P. de Zwart and J. Lucassen
items.note: New wage dataset from Gujarat to Bengal dating the Anglo-Indian divergence to the late seventeenth century, widening after the 1720s.

items.title: China, Europe, and the Great Divergence: A Restatement
items.who: S. Broadberry, H. Guan and D. D. Li
items.note: Replies to Peter Solar's critique, holding that China's leading region matched Europe's until the eighteenth century and that divergence began around 1700.

items.title: China: The Start of the Great Divergence
items.venue: Cambridge Economic History of the Modern World
items.note: Argues that Chinese output per head shrank after about 1740 as food production fell behind population growth.

items.title: Wage Earners in India 1500–1900: Regional Approaches in an International Context
items.note: Edited volume introducing previously unused wage material for several Indian regions and reinterpreting older data.

items.title: GLOBALISE: transcription of the VOC Overgekomen Brieven en Papieren
items.note: Project running 2022 to 2026 applying handwritten text recognition to over five million VOC pages, including Bengal and Coromandel records.

items.title: After da Gama: real wages in Western India, c. 1500–c. 1650
items.who: H. Carvalhal, J. Lucassen and P. de Zwart
items.note: Uses 2,710 wage observations from nine Western Indian locations to argue the gap with north-western Europe was visible by the early 1500s.

items.title: The long-run evolution of global real wages
items.note: Reviews two decades of comparative real-wage research, which places England and the Low Countries ahead of Asia from about 1720.

items.title: Wages, labour markets, and living standards in China, 1530–1840
items.note: Extends Chinese wage series back to 1530 and finds the Lower Yangzi–England wage gap widening after 1700.

items.title: Weak data nullify bold claims about economic trends in Qing China
items.note: Argues that plausible error margins on Qing grain output allow stable, rising or falling output per head, undermining claims of decline.

items.title: Real wages around the world: Insights from linear programming and accounting for climate differences
items.who: M. Moatsos and P. de Zwart
items.note: Recomputes real wages for 86 markets with climate-adjusted, cost-minimising baskets, shifting levels and trends in the Great Divergence comparisons.

items.title: Wages of Men, Women, and All the Others: Comparisons of the Standard of Living Based on Welfare Ratios Must Consider Household Complexity
items.note: Shows that male-wage welfare ratios overstate gaps where complex households relied less on the head's income than nuclear English ones.

items.title: Economic trends in Qing China: A response to Rawski's bold claims
items.who: S. Broadberry, H. Guan and D. D. Li
items.note: Rejects Rawski's wider error margins and argues that other indicators support declining per capita grain supply after 1700.

items.title: Long-run housing price indices and determinants: New data from Huizhou, China, 1570–1949
items.note: Builds housing price indices from over 1,000 Huizhou transaction contracts, showing the price evidence these documents can yield.

items.title: Agricultural growth in the Yangzi Delta: 1393–1953
items.note: Long-run reconstruction of Yangzi delta agricultural output bearing on the region's income trajectory before and after 1700.

items.title: Innovation and the great divergence
items.note: Argues north-west Europe passed the Yangzi delta only after 1700, but that the opposing trends were continuations of paths begun in the fourteenth century.
